name: liquid S8 at 387 K (a constant index)
paper: H. Becquerel, "Recherches expérimentales sur la polarisation rotatoire magnétique", Ann. Chim. Phys. (5) 12 (1877) 5–87, for the index
source: the archive.org scan of Ann. Chim. Phys. (5) 12, https://archive.org/details/s696id13665280 (public domain mark): its text, SHA-256 8020c247086bffe4a9a7a58d0d08ddf4815ed2b19c5f8b1421bfbfc85891a458, and its page image n36 (p. 37), SHA-256 60b9e263de0cd6061d8e1b83d5e8687d5159bbe2c0a0d246bdf2380e86c417b1, fetched 2026-10-14: n = 1.9290 with the sodium D lines for "Soufre fondu (114 degrés)" (Tableau n° 2), read in an iron prism as the melt began to crystallise; the hotter, dark-yellow melt read 1.890 a little before (pp. 25–26), a rise of 0.039 on cooling that expansion is too small to explain, as Becquerel finds for the magnetic rotation. No open measurement of molten sulphur's visible absorption, or of its dispersion, was found (R08.T5.g's search): Sasson and Arakawa 1986 (Appl. Opt. 25, 2675; n and k over 0.4–2.0 µm at 121–183 °C), Sasson et al. 1985 (Icarus 64, 368), Hosokawa, Matsuoka and Tamura 1994 (J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 6, 5273; the absorption coefficient over 130–450 °C), Bass 1953 (J. Chem. Phys. 21, 80) and Meyer et al. 1971 (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 93, 1034) are closed, as is Meyer 1976 (Chem. Rev. 76, 367), the finding aid; the open preprint of Meyer et al. 1971 (UCRL-19660, 1970) gives the red absorption edge's shift, about 23.6 cm⁻¹ per kelvin, but not its position, and refractiveindex.info, HITRAN's aerosol list and Kitzmann and Heng 2018's compilation hold no liquid sulphur
licence: one published index cited as a fact, from a public-domain volume; no data set is copied (decision-r08-t5d ruling 5)
reduction: a constant index: Becquerel's n at 589 nm, 1.9290, at every wavelength of 380–780 nm, with k = 0. Molten sulphur's dispersion and its blue absorption edge, which makes the melt yellow at its melting point and dark red at its boiling point (Meyer et al. 1971), are not drawn, so a sulphur lake draws too white in the blue. 387 K stands for Becquerel's 114 °C
standIn: a constant index: liquid S8's real index at 589 nm near its melting point, 1.929 with no dispersion and k = 0, since no open measurement of the liquid's visible absorption was found; its blue absorption edge is not drawn
